# Slopapotamus...

## Posted on October 26, 2026

It is a very strange time to be in the music software business. We've been at this for nearly 25 years, which makes us very old-school indeed, and we've been through some pretty big changes, but nothing like what is occurring. If it was one thing, we could probably deal with it, but this AI... uh... event? is more like a hydra. One head takes the form of direct competition, of a sort. Not two weeks after we released AD-202 , there were two virtually identical releases; one of them was "modeled" directly from the code in our web demo. There are several more now. It's easy to tell when something is a one-shot vibe-coded job, because the marketing copy takes that particularly weird combo of hubris and brown-nosing that both Claude and ChatGPT models seem to be unable to avoid. We obviously can't really complain about AD-202 being ripped off, because it is itself a re-imagining of someone else's product. But still, we get the fun task of essentially competing against ourselves. This is, let me tell you, a real hoot. The next head took a while to really blossom, but this late bloomer has taken a top spot for pure annoyance: the cold ask. On any given day in the last month, we receive between 10 and 20 requests for "collaboration" or "partnership." 100% of them are AI generated, and they all follow a fairly simple formula: "hey, I was examining your site, and I think your [$PRODUCT] is really a stellar example of [$CATEGORY], and furthermore something something iLok." ChatGPT loves quoting our own web pages back to us, so these letters almost always have copy lifted directly from the front page of this site. They then go on to espouse the virtues of a "collaboration" with the sender. Traditionally, we have gone through the provided links and at least saw if there was a fit. In the case of a simple NFR request of a single product, even if the person asking didn't have a ton of followers, we would generally grant that as long as their aim was reviewing and not using. But we'd only get one or two a week normally. Now, if I vetted every sender, it's literally all I would do. So we have essentially stopped even bothering to read them. It is worth noting that every indie plugin dev has, by necessity, become extremely good at spotting AI-generated writing. The third head of this hydra is the endless amusement that techbros apparently get from kneecapping the music business. This tiny little business that, in its entirety would fit inside the toilet paper budget for one of the Magnificent 7, is continually the target of "can we replace them with code?" Rather than doing something useful like making insurance companies superfluous, Google (GOOGLE?!?!?!) somehow sees fit to devote actual product cycles to killing the plugin business. Like, there is literally nothing we can do about that. I'm reminded of Loki's comment in the first Avengers movie: "an ant has no quarrel with a boot." I honestly don't know why these people are so fascinated with killing off this industry, but empirically, they keep pursuing that end. The fourth head is the pivot of value. This one is hazier, and I don't know where it's going to shake out. Different plugin devs have different metrics for their own worth, and I don't presume to speak for them, but for us, we believe the value we provide is in our deep and extensive knowledge of DAWs, plugins, and music making, and how those three things interact. There are a lot of delay plugins. You buy ours because you believe that we either do understand, or want to understand, what you're trying to accomplish, and we want to help you realize it. You are paying for a relationship with Adam and I, in essence, and the fact that between the two of us we have nearly a century of experience in electronic music, and also use these tools we make. Our 25 or so years of business have been predicated on that relatively simple relationship, but the times, they are a-changin'. There is a lot that goes in to a marquee product, and we and our long-suffering testing crew work for actual months on every product to ensure that it is relatively problem free when it reaches you, does what it says on the tin, and will almost certainly be around in a decade, for whatever form your personal music-making device takes. To be clear, I'm not whining. If there wasn't a desire for flash-in-the-pan one-shots, they wouldn't exist. I would just say caveat emptor . We know what goes in to ensuring a plugin works in every format, on every operating system. As a consumer, you should be extremely skeptical of any company who sprang in to existence in the last six months, and suddenly has six products. All that said, we are proud of what we do, and I personally look forward to each workday, despite the gruff facade I put up. We are not asking for pity or anything, but we are legitimately worried for this business we love and the ecosystem we helped, in our small way, to create. It will, without question, be different in the coming months. There's no way around that. It remains to be seen whether it will be here at all. That's really on you, the customer. Do you want to trade dependability for cost and become your own quality assurance engineer? The decision is, as it always has been, yours. Chris Randall Bellows Falls, Vermont
